#10760. Google’s new ‘Fast Switch’ feature leaks, lets you use one number on two Android phones

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly.

Other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”

There are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

This would make my decision to buy device like Clicks Communicator much easier

As per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

On Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

#10758. Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10755. How to Use IP Geolocation to Stop Bots and Fraud (Without Hurting UX)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Several methods can help you deal with online threats and strengthen security. All are effective, but each has a trade-off. For example, the harder you make it for bots to affect your website’s performance, the more likely you are to frustrate real customers.

Those of you who browse online daily know that credential stuffing, fake signups & payment fraud keep growing. To prevent fraud, businesses install CAPTCHAs & hard blocks that treat bots and legitimate users the same, diverting them to your competitors.

IP geolocation maps an IP address to a physical location & network details, letting you spot suspicious traffic before it reaches sensitive actions. Used well, it’s an invisible, low-friction risk signal. In this guide, you will learn how to flag high-risk activity and apply soft geo-fencing with step-up authentication.

Today, an IP lookup returns far more than a country & city. It can also reveal several other parameters, like

Each of these fields acts as a clue telling who is really behind a request.

This data powers anomaly detection. You can start by building a baseline for normal behavior for each user with aspects like

Then, you can watch for deviations from that pattern. An attacker won’t look like the account’s real owner, so you'll catch them.

Geolocation makes several common attack patterns easy to spot:

The first is traffic bursts from data center ASNs. These are bots, as real customers don’t browse from cloud servers

Many accounts created from one IP or subnet. This is a clear sign of fake signups

Impossible travel, such as logins from two distant locations within minutes

Timezone vs. IP mismatch. A device’s clock disagrees with its apparent location.

Note: Geolocation is just a signal, not a verdict. VPNs, travel, & mobile carriers can all create false alarms, so it works best when combined with other signals. That’s exactly why a proportional, soft response beats a hard block.

In short, IP geolocation turns a bare IP address into context, helping you separate real users from automated or fraudulent traffic.

Not every IP geolocation anomaly deserves the same response. The simplest way to stay consistent is to define a clear risk-signal framework.

That can be a short list of checks. Each check can have a weight that reflects how strongly it suggests fraud.

With risk scoring, you can turn these checks into a decision. You just have to assign each signal a numeric weight.

For example, medium can be 10 & 30 can be high.

Now, you need to add up every signal that comes up & map the total to thresholds like

A single medium signal passes quietly, but several can trigger action.

If you treat this as an automatic block, it would punish legitimate customers. Instead, let it raise the score & you take action only if it stacks with other signals, like a hosting IP or a new device.

Now that you know how to quantify the risk, here is how you can protect yourself without damaging UX.

Before soft, let us learn about hard blocking. This is where you completely deny or permanently ban traffic from specific geographic regions.

Now, hard blocking by country may look effective, but it can backfire quickly. Here is how.

In the worst case, determined bot operators simply rotate to IPs in allowed regions, so the only people you stop are your real customers.

This is where the balance between security and user experience becomes critical. As the digital strategist and Founder at LawRank, Mariano Rodriguez emphasizes, "Your website's security should be a silent guardian, not a roadblock. If your fraud prevention creates friction, you aren't just stopping bots—you're turning away real clients. True digital trust is built when backend protections are seamless and invisible to the legitimate user."

Now, with soft geo-fencing, you can respond to risk proportionally instead of making a simple allow-or-deny call. Instead of totally banning the users, you adjust the level of friction to match the risk score from the previous section:

**Note: **For soft geo-fencing, passkeys are safest because they are phishing-resistant. Only a legitimate user can take the biometric tap and pass.

Before we start, let’s understand Express.js middleware. An Express.js middleware for Geolocation Risk Scores is a custom or 3rd party function that intercepts the incoming HTTP requests, extracts the client's IP address, fetches a security risk profile based on their geographic location & attaches that data to the request object (req) before it reaches your route handlers.

Here is how you can use it for fraud prevention and bot mitigation:

Note: You can make it stronger by adding velocity checks (too many attempts from one IP or account) & device fingerprints.

From a broader angle, IP geolocation isn't the final verdict. It is just a signal. But with this signal, you can score each request, respond in proportion to the risk & save hard blocks for clear abuse. This increases the friction for bots and keeps the flow easy for legitimate users.

#10754. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10752. Samsung’s Galaxy S27 redesign is ‘100%’ confirmed, leaker says – do you like it? [Poll]

Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series is getting a redesign, with a reliable leaker saying it’s definitely happening. But, do you like it?

To say that Galaxy smartphone design has been stale is a bit of an understatement. The same core design has been in use for over half a decade at this point, with only the smallest tweaks in the past few generations. And it’s been a problem, too. While Samsung insists that the vertical triple camera array is the company’s “core identity,” it also means that the industry’s move to magnetic wireless charging and accessories are essentially incompatible with Galaxy devices.

We’ve seen repeated leaks of the Galaxy S27 series so far with a new full-width camera island on the Ultra and Pro models, and leaker Ice Universe says that this design is now “100%” confirmed, with the final design having two larger camera lenses on the left side, a smaller lens on the bottom right, and a flash above that. We saw this same design in a leak earlier this month, which Ice said at the time was “wrong,” presumably because the flash was replaced by a fourth camera in the dummy unit.

But the question at this point is, do you even like this new look?

Personally, I’m on the fence. I’m thrilled Samsung is finally doing away with the table-rocking, Qi2-ruining vertical array, but I’m not exactly happy we’re getting an iPhone clone as a result. I’d say beggars can’t be choosers, but this is Samsung we’re talking about – I think it’s fair to ask for a bit more.

#10750. XREAL Aura Initial Review: Taking Android XR out of the headset, but who is it for?

We all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we? Almost everyone can relate to that futuristic sense of wonder that comes from the movies where we see digital elements being interacted with through a simple wave of the hand. To date, that’s only really been replicable through big ol’ headsets like Apple’s Vision Pro or the various Meta Quest sets. But with XREAL Aura, Android XR brings that feeling to something far easier to actually use, but my one remaining question is who this product is for.

XREAL isn’t new to the mixed reality space. The company has been building some of the best example of optical see-through XR glasses. These aren’t quite like a VR headset because they actually let you see the world around you, not through a camera, but by simply making the lenses themselves see-through. I’ve tried these in the past and, while they’re great for mirroring a tablet or laptop for bigger screen (especially on airplanes), I did feel they were missing something.

The other half of the formula is a wired puck that provides battery power and the brains of Android XR. There’s no screen on the puck, just a status light, and it has USB-C out for the glasses as well as USB-C in for power and/or external devices. It also has a fingerprint sensor (are you hearing this Android tablet makers??) and a touchpad, the latter used as a secondary, far subtler input method within Android XR to supplement hand tracking.

Together, these two make a wonderful package for building a true mixed reality experience. The displays are plenty bright for even the brightest indoor conditions (frankly, it’d be insane to use these outside in my opinion, though a wide-open plane window may present a challenge), and the electrochromic dimming does a great job of blocking out most, but not quite all of the world around you. If you’re looking to be fully cut off from reality as you would with a VR headset, these aren’t for you. I did find some display elements, like smaller text, a little tough to focus my eyes on at times, but I have a feeling that’s more so me being overdue for an eye exam than it is the glasses themselves. There’s virtually no flicker in my usage, with only bright white backgrounds occasionally being a little overbearing, and everything is smooth with the 120Hz refresh rate.

Where this hardware really shines compared to a typical VR headset is in its design, and it’s what makes XREAL a perfect partner for Android XR. The glasses themselves weigh in at 95 grams, a mere fifth of the Meta Quest 3 and Samsung’s Galaxy XR, and up to 700 grams less than Apple’s Vision Pro. It’s comfortable for much longer periods of time and not nearly as annoying to actually put on either, as it just feels like putting on a pair of bulky sunglasses. They look a little goofy, obviously, but far less so than a full-on VR headset like any of those mentioned above. This is also the only one of those I consider “mixed reality” thanks to the see-through lenses. Apple and Samsung constantly talk about Vision Pro and Galaxy XR as if they’re mixed reality, but a camera feed is explicitly not true reality. But XREAL’s glasses still aren’t quite just augmented reality, because they’re not just letting you see that digital world through a tiny window, they’re quite literally overlaying everything on top of the real world around you. The illusion is somewhat broken by the limited 70-degree field-of-view and the fact that darker backgrounds often look a little funky when there are light sources in the real world in front of you, but I can say with confidence that this is my favorite version of this experience – the speakers are pretty good too, topping it all off.

Google’s platform launched on Samsung’s Galaxy XR headset earlier this year, and it’s all pretty familiar on XREAL Aura. The Android-based experience opens up to a floating launcher of your favorite apps that mostly open up into floating windows in front of you. You can use hand gestures to move everything around or interact with UI elements, and every app I tried worked perfectly well. The gestures can be hit or miss at times, especially the one for going back to the home screen (having this as a long-press that you have to physically look at your hand for gets annoying when doing anything remotely fast-paced, but thankfully the top button is a dedicated home shortcut), but it works well and everything is designed fairly intuitively. A floating cursor shows where you are aiming with a pinch acting as a tap on a touchscreen, and you can move things around in your space as if they’re real objects. There’s a sense of depth throughout the entire experience.

Some apps open to fully immersive experiences, but these are still in the minority. XREAL touts that there are around 150 experiences launching alongside Aura, but it’s definitely still early days here. Apps like Google TV should obviously be ready for a full format like that but, most things, like the Google Docs app which I’m typing this review in right now, just act as if they’re on independent displays floating around you.

Like Googlebook, Android XR is also still struggling to figure out the best app experience for each user. Most things are mobile apps, including Google Chrome which is just the standard Android version from your phone. It’s fine in most cases, but I found this restrictive seeing as I can get a ton done in a browser, but fighting mobile optimization is a frustrating way to interact with a window that can be as big as a TV if you want it to. Meanwhile, the Spotify app is weirdly the web version which is horribly optimized for interacting with hand gestures. I’d have rather had the mobile version here. Another quirk I found was notifications, which pop up at the top of the display and quite literally on top of whatever you’re doing. Something they were invasive, and having to physically reach out to dismiss them is a little annoying. I’m sure there are workflows to help make this less of a distraction, but I’d almost rather have notifications turned off entirely.

There’s also Gemini, which is core to the experience here. A quick “Hey Google” triggers a Gemini Live session for answering questions, and you can share what you’re seeing to give additional context. It’s way faster than switching between apps to get a quick search done, but there are friction points here, especially if you’re just asking a single question. Gemini answers quickly and leaves the conversation going, great for follow-up queries, bad if you’re done because the UI controls go away, which leaves you to tell Gemini to end the session which, every time, it asks for secondary confirmation you want to end. Google, if I say “end the session,” I think that should be more than sufficient proof I want to end the session. Luckily, a long-press of the top home button fixes that headache, but I still hate that I either need to use a physical control, or basically have to fight an AI to end a conversation that I started hands-free.

Performance is excellent. Everything is smooth and quick, probably thanks in part to XREAL’s use of 12GB of RAM alongside Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.

But how do you actually use a product like this?

That’s the question I found myself asking when I first spun up XREAL Aura and started to learn its ins and outs. See, other XREAL glasses have an extremely straightforward use case. Plug in the external device of your choice, get it on a bigger screen. Simple, easy, obvious. I found this helpful in travel primarily, with a bigger display for my MacBook feeling nice for tasks like video editing, while the main value came in just having a very comfortable way to watch a movie on a flight from my connected tablet.

Both of those use cases are valid on XREAL Aura. You can plug a USB-C device into the puck to get that wired mirroring through an Android XR window, and it works super well. Having Android XR alongside that mirroring also opens the door to added functionality, like having extra windows off to the side for perhaps a media app or reference document if you run out of room on the wired device. As just one example, I kept Spotify and Slack open in side windows while using Aura with my MacBook Air for an afternoon of writing articles.

I think Android XR makes Aura an absolute powerhouse for media consumption, as you can just download content directly to the device (256GB of storage in the base model) for a flight, or even just use streaming apps if you have Wi-Fi. I couldn’t find any 3D content during my brief review period (nothing in my Google TV library was compatible, apparently), but that’s also on the table. Genuinely, I cannot wait to use these on my next long flight.

But outside of those, I think a lot of the other scenarios start to fall apart.

By far the most popular use case for virtual/mixed reality has been gaming. XREAL Aura has a ton of potential here and I’m really excited to try out Project Hail Mary: Journey to the Stars on this, but the fact that these are simply glasses restricts a lot of what you can do. Any big movements could easily result in the glasses slipping or even falling off, whereas a VR headset is much more secure. Stationary immersive gaming has potential, and XREAL’s Gamesir controller collab shows promise, but I’m just not sold on these as a replacement to something like Meta Quest seeing as the latter already has a deep catalog of games and a much more affordable price.

The other use case is productivity, one I’m also not entirely sold on. As mentioned, this entire post was written in Aura, and I’m not sure I benefitted much from that experience versus just using a normal laptop or desktop computer. My workflow was having Google Docs up in the center, typing on a physical keyboard (only a psycho could use the virtual keyboard for anything beyond the shortest messages or passwords) with reference documents in Chrome off to my right and Slack on my left, with the occasional “Hey Google” command helping to find information on the fly (such as the weight comparison earlier). It all works well, but I think Android XR is inherently limited by its reliance mostly on mobile apps, and also just by the use of gestures. You can use a mouse or trackpad, of course, but at that point you might as well just use a laptop.

XREAL Aura is for a very specific customer from my point of view. Wired mirroring is still very much the strong suit here, with Android XR’s apps and offline video giving these utility outside of just relying on another device. That was my problem with previous XREAL glasses, because the experience just varies wildly depending on what’s connected. Aura’s puck and Android XR experience solves every complaint I had about previous models, while expanding very much on what it can do.

Further limiting matters is the price. $1,279, in my book, is actually a mostly fair price for this, especially given the RAMageddon of it all. XREAL 1+ Pro come in around $600 and is utterly useless without a secondary device. XREAL Aura more or less doubles the price, but includes the best possible version of that secondary device while also giving you the added camera sensors that are only available as add-ons for other hardware. Don’t get me wrong, it’s still pricey, but I don’t think it’s unfair either, especially not when one of the main competitors for this sort of experience is still $3,600 (which still sounds insane two years later, even for Apple).

We’ll have far more to say about XREAL Aura in a long-term review from our Nick Sutrich, but the verdict on day one is that Android XR has really solved the biggest problem for XREAL, while XREAL has solved a lot of big problems for Android XR, all while being an overall win for the user at the end of the day. Not so often we get a storybook ending like that in tech anymore, and I’m all here for it.

Don’t forget, XREAL Aura is $200 off – so $1,099 – through the end of December. Much more worth it at that price.

Turns old Game Boy cartridges into a chiptune jukebox.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new device on Kickstarter claims to make Game Boy cartridges relevant again by playing soundtracks from your favorite classic Nintendo games. The Retro Song Bird is a box-shaped speaker that supports Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges, with support for over 1,900 games. Simply inserting a cartridge into the speaker gives you access to all soundtracks and sound effects, which can be controlled using onboard physical controls including next, previous, and volume.

The Retro Song Bird also comes with a 3.5mm stereo line-out and a USB Type-C port in case you want to connect to other audio equipment. According to the developer, it offers accurate, register-level sound emulation and can be used to sample and remix music from your Game Boy cartridges. It exposes all four audio channels (two square, wave, noise) as separate USB audio streams that can be imported into a DAW. This allows you to isolate individual melodies, waveforms, and sound effects from old games to create your own melodies. There’s even support for LSDj for playing saved chiptune tracks, while two Retro Song Bird units can be synced for DJ-style performances using Game Boy cartridges instead of traditional records.

In addition to playing retro video game soundtracks, the Retro Song Bird also supports the Game Boy Camera, allowing you to use it as a webcam offering a glorious 128×112 pixels resolution and 5 frames per second speed. Other features include the ability to back up and restore save files, ROMs, flash writable carts, and export any soundtrack or sound effect as WAV onto your PC. The listing also includes other abilities, including an Alarm Mode, a record of every cartridge you've ever plugged in, an open API for developers, and over-the-air updates.

The Retro Song Bird is currently available to back on Kickstarter, with the standard model starting at $79. The introductory $59 Early Bird offer has already sold out, while the developer is also offering a two-unit bundle for $150. Shipments are expected to begin in April 2027.

The developer notes that only a handful of hand-assembled prototypes currently exist and that the hardware and design still need some refinements. The project also faces potential manufacturing challenges, including component availability, finding suitable manufacturing partners, and producing injection-molded enclosures. Like any other Kickstarter campaign, delivery timelines are subject to change, and backers should be aware that there is no guarantee the finished product will ship as planned.

#10747. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

#10746. Oppo may finally be fixing broken 3rd-party launchers with ColorOS 17

Most Chinese-brand Android phones don’t like it when you use a 3rd-party launcher, but the ColorOS 17 update may be changing that.

If I hop on a phone from Oppo, Vivo, Honor, or most other Chinese brands and try to use a 3rd-party launcher, I’m definitely not going to like how the phone operates. Often, there’s a weird delay when navigating back home or opening the Overview multitasking screen. Sometimes, Overview doesn’t work at all, essentially forcing you back to the default launcher that shipped with the phone.

But one Reddit user says Oppo is doing things differently in the ColorOS 17 update. According to their experience, the delay and other issues with 3rd-party launchers are completely solved. OnePlus’s OxygenOS doesn’t have the same issues, so it’s good to see that OnePlus users who are still set to receive ColorOS 17 in the near future won’t feel like their phones are losing a valuable feature.

Chinese Android brands like Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi, Realme, and several others often outshine Western brands in many ways, but they’ve always had one annoying weakness: software. Whether it’s the number of updates a phone receives, overall quality, or another specific issue, Chinese brands often build very different visions of Android than Google, Samsung, Motorola, or Nothing.

The value and hardware prowess these phones usually deliver help outshine software weaknesses, and these companies have been steadily improving software over the past year or two to meet the demands of a more Westernized audience. Companies like Honor now offer 7 years of software updates, and ColorOS is widely regarded as the best Android skin next to Samsung’s One UI in many circles. That’s great news for everyone, especially in an age where fewer smartphone companies compete for your hard-earned dollars.

#10744. Google Voice app gets a redesign on Android, and it screams RCS [Gallery]

Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a new app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a big neon sign that says “RCS is coming.”

Google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

That might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

The new look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

Material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field.

The most important thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent update directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.

#10742. 5 Best AI Anime Video Generators in 2026, and Are AI Anime Videos Worth Making?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI video generators can now turn a prompt or a character image into a few seconds of animation, and anime is one of the most popular styles people ask for. But anime is also one of the hardest styles to get right: flat colors, thin linework and stylized motion expose the weaknesses of video models quickly. For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

This article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

We reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

AI anime video generator by Pollo AI sits within a general AI video platform. On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

Limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

Fits: creators who want image, video and editing tools in one platform and are comfortable testing results before committing.

Vidu lists text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video modes. For image-to-video you can set first and last frames. Reference-to-video lets you upload several images of a character, object or scene, and saved references can be reused through a My References feature. The site highlights 2D animation and diverse artistic styles, mentions 1080p output and offers an API platform aimed at enterprise use.

Strengths for anime work: the clearest set of consistency tools among the five pages we reviewed, with first and last frames, multi-image references and reusable saved characters.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not specify clip durations beyond examples, detail its anime-specific templates, or list prices. Free credits are mentioned without an amount.

Fits: sequences built around a recurring character, and teams that want an API.

Kling AI presents Kling 4.0 for video, described as offering stable dynamic motion and an audio-visual experience, alongside an image model, a Motion Control tool and a node-based Canvas editor for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video. It also lists MCP and CLI support for batch generation and automated production, and an API platform with documentation.

Strengths for anime work: motion-focused tooling and a workflow environment for storyboards and multi-step production, plus automation options for developers.

Limitations and gaps: the page we reviewed does not detail image-to-video specifics, first and last frame controls, camera control, durations, video resolution or pricing, and it gives no anime-specific guidance.

Fits: teams that value motion control and scripted or batch pipelines.

Hailuo AI, from MiniMax, describes creating AI videos and images from text or photos. Its page shows a reference field and an Omni Reference option, a banner for a model that mentions multimodal generation and editing, and many photo-based templates such as photo-to-motion, transformation and style transfer.

Strengths for anime work: an accessible, template-driven way to animate a still image and try stylized effects quickly.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not explain how reference works, or state camera control, durations, resolution, API availability or pricing. Template-driven results may be harder to control precisely than prompt- and frame-driven workflows.

Fits: quick experiments and social clips made from a single image.

Dreamina describes itself as an all-in-one creative platform for images, videos and talking avatars. For video it lists text-to-video, image-to-video, sketch-to-video, cartoon video generation and reference-to-video, using several Seedance models, along with editing examples such as green-screen replacement. It also offers image generation and upscaling.

Strengths for anime work: a broad toolset, including cartoon-oriented generation, references and editing in one environment.

Limitations and gaps: no official maximum duration or video resolution is stated, and the page notes that displayed pricing is for reference only and that final pricing requires signing in. The breadth of features and models can make it harder to know which one to use for a given shot.

Fits: creators who want images, video and avatars under one roof.

“Not stated” means the vendor page we reviewed did not say, not that the feature does not exist. Treat the table as a checklist of questions to answer in your own tests.

It depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

Treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”

Scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

Developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

The script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

Video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below shows the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

Most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

Usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

Partly. Reference images, saved characters and shared keyframes help, but you should still review every shot for drift.

For short clips, concept previews and storyboards, often yes. For long, dialogue-driven stories, not yet.

It depends on the tool and plan. Read the current terms and make sure you have rights to any characters or assets you upload.

Run the same character image and prompt through each, then compare consistency, line stability, motion quality and cost per usable second.

AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

#10740. A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds

Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling

To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."

This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."

In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
