#10700. WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

“WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta update, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.

#10698. The Design Workflow Is Broken. Here Is How Vitalii Khomenko Thinks It Should Be Fixed

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

With 250+ client engagements across both agency and embedded in-house roles, Vitalii Khomenko has seen product teams from the inside in a way few designers have. Here he makes the case for a new kind of design workflow built for the AI era, and explains why the window to adapt is narrower than most founders think.

For the last decade, every startup conversation about speed eventually became a conversation about engineering. Hiring more developers, cutting scope, choosing a simpler stack, it was almost always a dev-side problem. Vitalii Khomenko, Principal Designer at Orizon Design and founder of Fluente LLC, argues that's no longer true. And he has a specific view on what teams should do instead.

What makes Khomenko's perspective worth taking seriously isn't just seniority. It's the specific shape of his experience. Over a career spanning 250+ client engagements, he has worked both as an external specialist brought in to deliver and as an embedded designer who became the single connective thread between product, brand, and execution. That dual vantage point is rare. Most designers live on one side of that line. Khomenko has operated extensively on both, which gives him an unusually clear read on where friction actually originates inside product teams, and where it doesn't.

His work spans early-stage startups finding their first visual language and established brands managing complex, multi-disciplinary design systems. Across that range, certain patterns repeat. And the pattern that started becoming impossible to ignore this year pointed him toward a conclusion that is reshaping how he thinks a modern design workflow should actually be structured.

The bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved. And the workflow needs to move with it.

When shipping code was slow, the existing design workflow made sense. Multiple rounds of revision, user testing, iteration, all of that fit naturally into the window while engineering caught up. That window is now gone, and most design workflows were never updated to reflect it.

"Founders are asking design teams to move at the same speed as an AI-assisted dev pipeline, and design doesn't compress the same way code does," Khomenko says. The result is a workflow that was built around a constraint that no longer exists, applied to a pipeline that has fundamentally changed around it.

The forced choice between polish and speed that product teams are now navigating isn't new as a concept. What's new is how stark it has become, and how directly it traces back to a workflow problem rather than a people problem. "Because development is cheap and fast now, there's constant pressure to ship the next thing immediately," he explains. "But the products that actually retain users are still the ones where the details were considered carefully. Fewer revision rounds isn't a process improvement if it means shipping avoidable friction."

Khomenko has watched this play out across enough teams, at enough stages, to be specific about where the existing workflow breaks down. The issue isn't design judgment. It's where that judgment sits in the process, and what format it's expected to produce at the end.

To understand Khomenko's proposed fix, it helps to understand exactly where the current workflow stalls. For most product teams, the end of the design process looks like this: a designer produces polished, dev-ready screens inside Figma, and hands that file to engineering. Engineering then interprets those screens, translates the visual decisions into code, and builds from there.

That translation step, Figma file to working code, is where the pipeline now breaks down. AI-assisted engineering has made the building part dramatically faster. But the translation step hasn't changed. An engineer still has to read a Figma file, interpret spacing, extract assets, make judgment calls about component structure, and write the implementation from scratch. That process takes the same amount of time it always did.

"The manual workflow inside Figma simply isn't keeping up with AI-boosted engineering," Khomenko says. "The design handoff is quietly becoming the thing everyone is waiting on."

The result is a pipeline where everything around the handoff has accelerated, and the handoff itself has become the single point of drag. Figma, in other words, was built for a world where engineering was the slow part. It wasn't designed to feed a pipeline where engineering moves at AI speed.

This is the core of what Khomenko is proposing, and it's a more significant structural shift than it might first appear.

In his workflow, Figma doesn't disappear. It moves. Rather than serving as both the exploration environment and the final delivery artifact, Figma becomes the visual exploration layer exclusively: the place where brand identity is established, layout logic is worked through, and design direction is validated. It remains the right tool for figuring out what something should look and feel like.

But the final delivery, the artifact that actually goes to engineering, is code. Specifically, components built into prepared libraries that engineering can work from and scale directly, without any translation step in between.

The difference in implementation speed is the point. When a designer delivers a coded component library rather than a Figma file, engineering doesn't need to interpret anything. The decisions are already expressed in the language they're building in. What previously required an engineer to read, interpret, and re-create from a visual reference now arrives ready to use. In a pipeline running on AI-assisted development, that difference compounds fast.

"Figma is still the right place to explore what something should look and feel like," Khomenko says. "But handing over a Figma file and asking engineering to implement it is now the slow path. Delivering in code is the fast path. That's the shift."

Executing this workflow requires a different kind of designer, and Khomenko is direct about that. The UI/UX designer becoming a Design Engineer is, in his assessment, not a distant possibility. It is a matter of time, and the teams treating it as a future consideration rather than a present reality are the ones most likely to find themselves stuck at the handoff.

But Khomenko is equally clear about what this shift doesn't mean. Delivering in code is one part of the role, not the whole of it. The full design cycle isn't going anywhere. Applying branding to imagery, producing animations, building marketing materials, these remain essential creative tasks that require a broad and varied toolkit well beyond code. "The designer of the near future isn't just generating code," he says. "They're moving across the full cycle, brand, motion, marketing, product, with design engineering as an important and growing part of that stack, not a replacement for it."

What changes is that code-ready delivery becomes a core expectation within that stack. The designer who can move fluidly from visual exploration in Figma to component delivery in code, while also carrying the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level users actually experience, is the profile that the new workflow demands.

Khomenko is candid that no single version of this workflow has fully standardized yet. Every team is figuring it out differently. The tools are evolving, the handoff expectations are shifting, and the processes teams are building around all of it vary considerably. There is no off-the-shelf playbook.

But this is precisely where his 250+ engagements become more than a credential. They're a dataset. Having watched enough teams, at enough stages, through enough cycles of tooling change, Khomenko can see through the noise of individual variation and identify what's directionally true even when the specifics are still in flux. "Each team's workflow is really custom at this stage," he says. "But some general patterns of how this is going to look in the near future are already visible."

Those patterns consistently point in the same direction: design judgment moving earlier, final delivery moving into code, and the designer's role expanding in technical range while staying broad in creative scope. The exact tools and sequences will keep shifting. The underlying logic of the workflow Khomenko is describing is already taking shape in the teams paying closest attention.

For founders and product leads, the workflow Khomenko is describing has direct implications for how teams are staffed, budgeted, and structured.

Front-load design judgment. The biggest leverage in the new workflow isn't faster execution, it's better problem definition before generation starts. Bring senior design thinking in earlier, when it can shape what gets built rather than polish what's already done.

Separate exploration from delivery. Figma and the visual exploration phase serve a distinct purpose from the final delivery layer. Treat them as separate stages with separate expectations, rather than collapsing them into a single step expected to produce everything.

Shift the delivery expectation to code. Whether that means hiring for Design Engineer range, developing it internally, or restructuring handoffs, the end of the design pipeline needs to arrive in a form engineering can work from directly. The translation step is where time goes to die, and it's now the most avoidable part of the process.

Protect the full creative stack. Design engineering matters more than it ever has. It is not, however, the whole job. Teams that reduce design to code generation will lose the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level users actually experience.

Stay flexible. The workflow is still forming. Teams that build rigidity into their process now will find themselves redoing that work within a year. The teams getting this right are the ones building enough adaptability into their structures to absorb what's still coming.

"The Figma handoff made sense when engineering was the slow part," Khomenko says. "Engineering isn't the slow part anymore. Delivering in code isn't the future of design workflow. For the teams paying attention, it's already the present."

I write about AI and software development from the angle that usually gets skipped: what a spec sheet or benchmark actually implies once you try to build with it. Find me on LinkedIn.

#10697. What other brands can learn from the success of ‘Grand Theft Auto’

Grand Theft Auto was once the game you weren’t supposed to own, let alone play. Today, it’s one of entertainment’s biggest cultural forces, as shown by its latest release, GTA VI, which is arguably the most anticipated game release ever, with $1 billion in preorders and countless memes as evidence.

So, how did something once treated as a threat to culture become such a powerful part of it?

As someone who has spent more years of their life playing GTA than not—and who now helps brands find their own loyal following—I think it offers a lesson in how creative conviction can become a commercial superpower.

What can we learn from the rise of Rockstar’s biggest player?

Culture moved. ‘GTA’ kept designing its way

The original top-down Grand Theft Auto launched on November 28, 1997. At the time, music, television, and film dominated cultural conversation and gaming was dismissed to a dark corner of teenagers’ bedrooms. It was counterculture. Today, that’s changed. There are an estimated 3.5 billion gamers globally, gaming shapes conversation more than people think, and it has become a destination where culture is built.

While its audience grew, and culture shifted, GTA kept designing a world that was unmistakably its own. Critically, GTA wasn’t just a game set in a version of American culture; it was a playable satire of it, exaggerated and, yes, often uncomfortable. It had an extraordinary way of bringing users in on the joke. Excess became the punch line. And brilliantly, it didn’t ask players to watch the joke from a distance. They could participate in it.

As gaming became more mainstream, GTA brought this irreverent perspective with it. Its audience boomed but it didn’t lose the qualities that made the property so distinctive more than two decades ago. Its eventual, yet incredible, gravitational pull ensured that culture started moving towards it.

A world with a point of view

When creatives talk about a “brand world,” we usually mean the things that make a business recognizable: language, art direction, behavior, and personality. Grand Theft Auto has always taken that idea very literally. It demonstrates how powerful the idea can be when every detail contributes towards the world it’s building. Its fictional advertising, radio stations, characters, and dialogue all see the world through the same warped lens. You can be driving across Los Santos, doing nothing useful, and still be experiencing the brand. The city keeps talking to you.

That world influenced the medium. GTA III helped set the template for a generation of open-world games, from Saints Row to The Getaway. But a city you can explore is one thing; a city that could only belong to GTA is another.

Look at its brands. Burger Shot, Sprunk, and Lifeinvader turn fast food, soft drinks and social media into material for satire. Their ads parody the desires, insecurities, and commercial nonsense of the real world, while making GTA’s fictional one feel more alive. The radio does something similar. Music, presenters, and commercials make a journey feel like time spent somewhere, rather than a loading screen with steering. A drive across town might take you past a Cluckin’ Bell billboard boasting that its chicken is “better than roadkill.”

Because the brands are fictional, GTA has the freedom to make the joke as uncomfortable as it needs to be. (You don’t have to ask the company you’re mocking to approve it.) Those design details give the city a voice, and give GTA a self-fulfilling identity that extends far beyond its logo and missions.

None of this feels like design tactics layered on top of the game. The point of view is the game.

Being risqué isn’t enough

Let’s talk about GTA’s attitude. It’s another part of the story that’s aged very well. Plenty of brands have attitude. But few can authentically maintain it. Being provocative might get people’s attention. But it won’t earn their loyalty if the experience doesn’t match. For me, GTA has repeatedly raised the bar for what an interactive world—and what a world-leading brand—can be.

Its reputation for creating exceptional experiences does an enormous amount of its marketing work; a trailer arrives and people examine it frame by frame, dissect the details, make predictions, and revisit earlier games. They’re excited because they know GTA will deliver on its promise.

That is the foundation beneath the swagger. And an important lesson for every brand trying to be bold.

You don’t need everyone to love you

During the COVID-19 pandemic, I taught Sarah Mei, my wife, to play PlayStation. (“Taught” might be taking too much credit.) Would she play GTA VI? It’s very unlikely. Too violent. Fair enough. Grand Theft Auto doesn’t have to resolve that objection to succeed. Removing everything someone dislikes wouldn’t necessarily improve the experience for the people who love it.

I’ve put hundreds of hours into GTA. That changes the relationship I have with it. A film might occupy an evening. But a game can become somewhere you spend months. You learn its geography, understand its rules, and develop habits within it. The attachment starts to resemble supporting a team. There’s history there. GTA Online took that further; the world became somewhere to return to, meet friends and make new memories. Not just something you buy, it’s somewhere you spend your time.

And it’s not for everyone. The point is, it’s been intentionally designed for someone.

Wanting in doesn’t mean belonging in

The same applies to potential partners. While a brand might feel comfortable associating with GTA, that doesn’t mean their presence makes sense. People have spent years getting to know GTA’s world, and assert that even a good tonal match isn’t always welcome. After all, what does a real brand add? Does it make the world richer, or remind me that someone has bought their way in?

Most brands want to be relevant to more people. The temptation is to broaden the message, soften the edges, and make room for everyone. GTA seemingly surmises that some things aren’t worth watering down.

‘GTA’ makes gaming better

What retains my attention is the feeling that there’s always more to discover, and understand. Easter eggs being uncovered years after release; the detail of San Andreas, NPC dialogue that might actually be too detailed; and the license to ignore the mission. It’s all world-building. GTA’s design delivers. And I trust that GTA will improve with every launch.

That’s what makes Grand Theft Auto, in my view, one of the best brands in the world, even if it’s not a brand in the traditional sense of the word. Not because everyone wants it, but because it knows every detail either earns attention or breaks the spell.

That’s a useful challenge for brand design. Brands are very good at making things people recognize, want, or expect. Many are poor at challenging us. Designed for everyone, but resonating with no one. Can we design brands that have a greater, stronger perspective? Brands we would miss? Or, even better, brands we could learn to love?

#10694. Nvidia says it’s ‘absurd’ to assume it predicted the agentic moment during Vera’s development

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

It turns out Nvidia doesn’t have a crystal ball, either.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials. Ian Finder, the head of Nvidia’s data center CPU business, pushed back on that criticism in a recent conversation with Tom’s Hardware Premium at SC26, calling the notion that Nvidia somehow knew about the agentic wave four years ago when Vera development began "absurd."

“There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right? Am I going to sit here and tell you that we have this magic crystal ball around the agentic moment? That would be absurd, right?” Finder said. “But what we do have as a company, and I think this has been proven out in our track record, is [that] we have design intuition.”

Instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU. Coming from the assumption that data centers and AI workloads are accelerated (and they largely are), Finder says the co-design approach on the CPU can start in a “conceptually simple space, like what kind of CPU do we need to keep the accelerator fed and happy?”

Although conceptually simple, Finder continually looped back to a particular word to describe aspects of Vera and, to a lesser extent, Grace. “Opinionated” is the word he used, which in the broader context of Vera’s design, shows up in two places. Grace, Finder says, introduced an opinionated memory system with Nvidia’s Scalable Coherency Fabric, while Vera extends that memory system while adding an opinionated microarchitecture, Nvidia’s Olympus core.

The picture Finder paints is one of Nvidia starting from scratch in this space, contrasting it with the “legacy constraints” of, presumably, Intel and AMD in particular, who have large pools of customers with specific needs. As we described in our original breakdown of the Olympus architecture in Vera, Nvidia’s goal doesn’t seem to be to steal market share from AMD and Intel, but rather to grab market share in a CPU space that’s vastly accelerating on the back of AI agents.

This “clean sheet of paper” approach, and Nvidia’s codesign, led to some natural assumptions about what the CPU should do. “If we have silicon that needs really, really great single-thread performance, [and] we also need concurrency, then we need to get there with IPC instead of frequency. We need to make sure we have good loaded memory latency. We need to make sure we have a lot of bandwidth, and you start to design something on a clean sheet of paper that's not encumbered by dollar-per-core economics.”

Although Finder was clear that Vera’s design didn’t explicitly center around the agents we see today, there were early indications of the workload. “To say that four years ago, when we started putting pen to paper on Vera, [that] we absolutely saw the agentic moment, would [not] be... something I would claim, but we were starting to see the beginnings of tool calling and things like that. We certainly knew what we needed from a head node, and we knew the overall shape of this problem.”

As you can see in our Vera CPU benchmarking, the chip doesn’t excel at every workload. And, from the data you can see in our recent AMD EPYC Venice benchmarking, the AMD camp has reclaimed some top spots in several benchmarks. Finder suggests that the superior memory bandwidth of Vera will play a much bigger role in the agentic future as these systems evolve to take better advantage of the compute available.

A portion of the AI industry is focused on tackling the problem of fully utilizing the GPU, Nvidia included. GPUs shouldn’t sit idle for very long (if at all) with the demand today, and they don’t. The challenge today is spinning up these agent sandboxes quickly, within milliseconds, so that the CPU isn’t sitting idle, either.

Finder provided an example of using a coding agent. If you’ve used a coding agent before, you’re probably familiar with this process. After prompting, the model will make several small tool calls to read and locate files, passing back to the model in between. These are tiny calls, almost negligible, and the vast majority of the time is spent in the model on the GPU. Then, it may start compiling and testing the project, which is much more bound by the CPU. The GPU, Finder says, isn't sitting idle during that time. It’s being leveraged for another purpose. Finder suggests “that very same thing is going to happen on the CPU.”

This “very interesting computer science problem,” as Finder described it, is being investigated by AI startups such as Daytona and E2B to spin up and close down agentic sandboxes in milliseconds. And serving more agents will naturally put pressure on the memory system, which is an area where Vera has an edge. “We built a product that does really, really well without such optimizations, but as a design point that really will lean into them when the industry starts to catch up to this,” Finder said.

Vera is a fascinating chip, regardless of what you think of it and how it’s presented in marketing materials (from Nvidia itself or elsewhere). Although Grace was the starting point internally, Vera has ridden the wave of agentic to become a much bigger player in the world of CPUs, and Nvidia has already announced that it will follow up with its Rosa CPU featuring the new Rigel microarchitecture. Vera is an opinionated CPU indeed, and time will tell if that opinion is correct.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

#10692. Your company needs a new capability. Should you build it, buy it, or partner for it?

Years ago, I made the case to the leadership of a global consumer electronics company that it should acquire a relatively young streaming-device company. The TV screen was becoming a dumb pipe, and the value was moving to the software that decided what viewers watched. Owning the startup would let the company keep making world-class TVs while extending its reach onto screens it didn’t make.

The internal teams disagreed. The company had deep hardware expertise, strong engineers, and its own smart TV software. Why buy what we could build? A few years later, the company shipped its own streaming device. It wasn’t as good as the one that the startup created, it never gained traction, and the project was shut down.

That young company went on to go public and become a leader in streaming.

The story pains me to share even now, but it’s one that gets told over and over by other businesses as they wrestle with the decision to build, buy, or partner. Artificial intelligence has accelerated the pace at which businesses can develop new products, enter new markets, and reach new customers. AI also exposes gaps in a company’s capabilities, so leaders are facing the build/buy/partner question more often. Many are defaulting to the wrong decision: build.

Why does a bias for building in-house persist? The reasons include overconfidence (“I just need four people and six months”), not-invented-here syndrome, and what I refer to as launch bias, or estimating what it takes to launch, not what it takes to run the capability.

Now businesses are hampered by AI overconfidence, or a belief that AI can reduce the costs and effort of building in-house. In fact, AI is changing the math, but not evenly. It has made prototypes dramatically cheaper, and the savings are real. But they’re front-loaded. Running a capability, which means maintaining, securing and improving it for years, still takes resources, and AI shrinks those costs far less than it shrinks the cost of a demo.

And unfortunately, all the other assumptions about building in-house seldom hold up. The people you thought you had get reassigned as other priorities take hold. And businesses confuse faster launch with effective ownership. By the time you realize you need to reconsider your approach, someone else has beaten you to market, or the project has lost internal mindshare.

Instead, you might be better off thinking like Ryan Gosling’s character Ryland Grace in Project Hail Mary, who realizes that saving humanity requires more than his own ingenuity. He needs a partner with capabilities he doesn’t possess. You may not need an alien ally, but you do need a map to guide you.

Before Choosing: Check Your Biases

Before deciding what to do, challenge your assumptions. Look three years out, accounting for the costs of building, maintaining, and improving the capability, not just launching it. Compare your last three internal builds against their original estimates for time, cost, and staffing. Establish a threshold for abandoning the effort before you start spending, so you don’t keep funding a bad decision. And ask someone without a stake in the outcome to challenge your thinking.

Build, Buy, or Partner?

The more strategic a capability seems to be, the more tempted you will be to own it. Importance is necessary, but not sufficient. If strategic importance were the be-all and end-all, every business would build its own oil refinery. A capability needs to be difficult for the competition to replicate and easy to integrate into your operations. In all, you should test the desired capability against four criteria: defensibility, time to value, integration risk, and cultural fit.

1. Is the capability defensible?

Does the capability create a durable moat and advantage that your customers notice? If the capability is easily commoditized and creates only a marginal improvement, building may not justify the investment.

2. How quickly do you need the value?

If you need to move quickly, do a reality check. Building might take too long, but acquiring a capability could be time consuming too, if doing so requires an acquisition. If your window is closing soon, you may need to partner with someone.

3. What is the integration risk?

Every option carries integration risk. When you build, the risk is ownership itself: compliance, maintenance, staffing, and a long tail of fixes. When you partner, you’re at the mercy of your partner’s capability development road map and factors out of your control, like the partner being acquired. With buying, you risk hidden technical debt, platform fragmentation, and culture clashes, which have harpooned many an acquisition.

4. What does the cultural fit look like?

This is an obvious question for a buy decision. Can you onboard and keep the people you need for the long run? But it’s also a potential challenge for a partner, with the additional wrinkle of managing potential competitive risks and building trust if your partnership is not exclusive.

At this point, clarity will emerge, and with clarity comes sensible decision making along these lines:

Build If: You are confident that the required capability is not only important but also creates a competitive wedge and customer loyalty for the long term, and you are willing to fund it for years.

Buy if: You need speed but don’t need to own the capability.

Partner if: You need speed and ownership of capability.

These choices aren’t necessarily permanent or mutually exclusive. You might partner first to enter the market and learn, then build or acquire once you better understand where the value lies. You’ll also notice I said nothing about AI in the framework. Defensibility, time to value, integration risk, and cultural fit address the same risks whether your engineers write every line by hand or generate a working demo over the weekend. AI changes the cost of starting. It doesn’t yet change the cost of owning.

The team I argued with could build a streaming device, and eventually did. What it couldn’t build was the position the startup already had. The next time someone tells you, “We can build that,” thank them for their confidence, and let them apply all the AI they want to build a prototype. Then ask to see year three.

#10690. Google confirms huge list of new Home features, including three Nest Thermostat upgrades

Google Home is constantly rolling out new updates and, today, the company is detailing some of its latest updates including a faster Gemini for Home experience and an upcoming Nest Thermostat upgrade.

In a post today, Google details several Google Home updates that are widely rolling out to users.

The first was announced last week – home keys in Google Wallet. This leverages compatible NFC and UWB (Aliro) locks on newer Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy smartphones, letting you unlock your door by simply tapping your phone.

Cameras are also getting an upgrade for Activity Zones:

…we’ve tightened Activity Zone boundary precision on our newest wired cameras to significantly reduce false alerts from passing cars, animals, and motion just outside your zone borders. We also redesigned the camera settings page to put Activity Zones front and center, and added a confirmation prompt on iOS when exiting an edited zone so you never accidentally lose your custom boundaries.

The Google Home website also gets faster scrubbing and new keyboard shortcuts – Left or Right arrow keys skip back or forward in 5-second increments, rapidly to jump 30 seconds or more.

Gemini for Home continues to get faster, with Google saying that the latest updates have resulted in an overall speed improvement of 20% on “everyday requests.” Gemini for Home has also expanded to six new countries including India, Taiwan, Singapore, Colombia, South Korea, and Brazil starting “next month.”

Finally, Google is also preparing some useful upgrades for Nest Thermostat.

The first is a dashboard for Nest Thermostat users in the US and Canada that shows “estimated cumulative savings” spurred by their thermostat. You’ll be able to see these savings in “the Climate space, thermostat controller, and Favorites widget.” The second is the abiltiy to use third-party room temperature sensors with the 4th-Gen Nest Learning Thermostat. Google has its own sensor for this that sells for $40, but there are more affordable alternatives that often bring more functionality too, so this is a really nice addition. Compatible brands will include IKEA, Eve, and Aqara.

Starting in December, Nest thermostat owners in the U.S. and Canada can check the app to see estimated cumulative savings. And they can also balance hot and cold spots with compatible third-party room sensors with their 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat.

A third update is to the Dynamic Farsight faces on the latest Nest Learning Thermostat. “New” faces are coming with “designs to match your aesthetics,” while a new Lunar face will track moon phases.

Dynamic Farsight already lets you see the time, temperature, weather, and air quality from across the room, and starting this December, we’re rolling out new Dynamic Farsight faces with designs that match your aesthetics. Keep an eye out for seasonal animations on the Temperature face, or switch to our new Lunar face to track the phases of the moon right on your wall.

#10689. Mental health’s short-term mindset problem

When I struggled with anorexia as an adolescent, I learned that the traditional healthcare ecosystem had a simplified view of recovery: stabilize vitals and clear the patient out to keep costs down.

Now, as an eating disorder treatment founder and CEO, I spend my days working with collaborative health insurance plans to fix these historical dynamics. Together, we’ve made incredible progress toward value-based care, a system that rewards treatment providers for getting patients better rather than for how often patients see them.

But as the mental health industry works to measure real clinical impact, providers and health plans share the same roadblock: overreliance on immediate, short-term financial ROI.

Because health plans and employers usually operate on 12- to 24-month budget cycles, standard financial models naturally hunt for quick wins, like preventing an ER visit within that same year. Behavioral health doesn’t fit into a short-term box.

This isn’t about bad intentions; it’s just how the financial system was built. In practice, though, it leaves out people managing on the outside who still need real support before things get worse.

THE STRUCTURAL CHALLENGE

Real health savings take time. We already spend money upfront to manage conditions like diabetes, because it prevents far more expensive health emergencies years later. Behavioral health needs that same long-term investment.

A major roadblock is that behavioral and physical health costs are tracked in separate silos. On paper, investing in mental health looks like an extra expense, even when it directly drives down physical healthcare costs, like expensive hospital admissions.

I lived this firsthand: I appeared as a “zero-cost” member on claims data until I was hospitalized, leading to months of treatment. Early intervention could have prevented immense suffering and expense, yet data shows nearly 40% of pediatric eating disorder patients first enter the healthcare system under general medical complaints rather than a behavioral health diagnosis. When hospitalization does occur, the median time from diagnosis to admission is under a month.

THE MYTH OF THE “LOW-RISK” MEMBER

The true cost of mental illness isn’t always apparent in claims data. For example, millions of people struggling with things like severe eating disorders, OCD, major depression, and anxiety arrive at work or school every day, meet their daily goals, turn in homework, and maintain a general outward appearance of being well.

Because they aren’t ending up in emergency rooms or generating high costs, they’re viewed as low-cost.

Evaluating mental healthcare strictly on one-year cost savings makes it hard to justify giving high-functioning people the full support they need. On paper, their immediate medical costs look minimal, so why invest in specialized care before something terrible happens?

Under standard short-term budget cycles, care is too often delayed until it becomes a crisis, costing both the person and their health plan much more in the long run.

CO-CREATE THE NEXT PHASE OF VALUE-BASED CARE

Health plans are the indispensable engine of healthcare innovation, and real systemic change happens only when health plans and care providers agree on incentives—something I’ve seen firsthand with some of the partners we work with at Equip. Moving beyond short-term cost containment toward long-term value on investment (VOI) requires new frameworks:

  • Health plan partnerships could look at whether people are regaining their lives—such as staying symptom-free, doing well at work, and feeling good—instead of just counting how many people stayed out of the hospital. 
  • Health insurance plans and employers can work together on long-term contracts, giving treatment the time it needs to pay off in real, cumulative savings.
  • Getting people help early keeps them healthy and stops small problems from turning into bigger ones. The crazy thing is, the current system only rewards fixing things after they break. So when someone actually steps up and chooses to get help, the system sees that as an extra bill instead of a huge win.

Fixing this doesn’t mean ignoring financial reality, but we need to look at the bigger picture together. To fulfill the promise of value-based care, we need models that match the reality of recovery.

Resilience should open doors to care, not close them, and together, we can build a healthcare system that keeps people well before they break.

Kristina Saffran is cofounder and CEO of Equip.

#10686. AI is today’s light bulb

In 2004, I set out to do something many in the energy business thought was crazy: digitize the last mile of the electric grid—the wires and meters between the substation and the homes and businesses it serves. My bet was that internet protocol, the common language of the world’s computers, would eventually connect the grid too. Once it did, every meter and sensor could talk to the software running it.

Plenty of smart people told me it would never happen. Utilities, like pipeline, rail, and water operators, plan in decades; they cannot afford to get reliability wrong. So the real work was finding the handful of utility leaders willing to go first.

Two decades later, more than three out of four electric meters in the United States are smart meters, over 128 million of them, according to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

I bring this up because I believe we are at the start of something much bigger now, that reaches beyond the grid to every system the economy runs on. AI is today’s light bulb: It’s what everyone can see. But the revolution is the network underneath it, and most leaders are looking at the wrong part.

EDISON’S REAL INVENTION WAS THE NETWORK

When Thomas Edison switched on his Pearl Street Station in lower Manhattan on September 4, 1882, he was selling light. Within a month, 59 customers were using it to light about 400 lamps. By 1884, it served more than 500 customers.

In The Age of Edison, historian Ernest Freeberg shows that what remade American cities wasn’t the light bulb itself but what it required. Every building needed a wire, and every wire needed a power supply behind it. Once that network was in place, it outgrew its first purpose almost immediately. Electric light, along with the electric elevator, allowed buildings to grow. Factories ran through the night. Cities stayed awake after dark.

Then came the unexpected uses. The first household appliances had nowhere to plug in, so people screwed fans and irons into the sockets hanging from their ceilings. In 1904, Harvey Hubbell patented a separable plug that made the connection safer and simpler. Manufacturers kept selling incompatible designs for years before settling on the parallel-blade shape that Hubbell patented, still in your wall today.

Safety rules came about the same way. According to Freeberg, insurance companies, tired of paying for electrical fires, pushed the electric companies into agreeing on the first common standards.

Once the plug was standard, anyone could build something that used it. Refrigerators, radios, washing machines, and eventually computers all came through that same wire. The light bulb may have started it, but the network built the twentieth century.

THE NETWORK IS THE PLATFORM

For more than a century, the grid’s job was to move power, while pipelines, rail lines, ports, and water systems moved physical goods. Increasingly, every one of those systems also has to move data. Every device connected to critical infrastructure, from a car charger to a data center to a pipeline valve or a rail switch, is becoming a device that sends and receives information.

AI deserves the excitement it’s getting today. But it only creates value when it can reach the equipment it’s meant to run. For utilities, pipelines, and water systems, that means the network is no longer back-office plumbing. It’s the platform every new capability will run on.

The network itself is changing. Satellites are beginning to connect directly to the devices ground networks serve, so a sensor on a pipeline far from any tower can be reached from above. The most valuable networks will work on the ground and in orbit as one, and the licensed airwaves connecting them will be among the economy’s scarcest resources.

THIS IS BIGGER THAN THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION

I realize that being bigger than the Industrial Revolution is a bold claim. The Industrial Revolution gave machines the power to do physical work. What is happening now gives machines the ability to decide and act on work as it happens, like software that spots a fault on a power line and reroutes electricity around it before customers notice. The same shift is coming to pipelines, rail lines, ports, and water systems.

It is also moving much faster. Electricity took half a century to reach most American homes. The smart meter transition took about two decades. This one will be measured in years. The network decisions infrastructure companies make now will decide which of them can take part.

WHAT THE WINNERS HAVE IN COMMON

Robert Metcalfe, who co-invented ethernet, observed that a network’s value grows with the square of the number of devices on it. Think of the fax machine: One is worthless, but each machine added makes the others more valuable. The same is true of the networks running critical infrastructure. The devices on them wear out and get replaced. A well-built network keeps carrying whatever comes next, for decades.

Nobody in 2004 was talking about AI. The utilities that built those smart grid networks are among the best positioned to use it now. Pipeline, rail, port, and water operators now face the same choice. The operators that wait will have to retrofit—tearing open the walls to run wire that should have been there from the start, and paying more for it.

And the winners plan for a network without edges, one that reaches a city substation and a remote pipeline, so they never have to bolt it on later.

HERE WE GO AGAIN

I was called crazy in 2004 for saying the grid would run on a network. I expect some people will say the same thing now when I say networks will run all the infrastructure the economy depends on.

Edison thought he was selling light. He was founding a century of infrastructure and innovation. Whoever builds the networks now, on the ground and in orbit, is founding the next.

Scott Langis president and CEO of Anterix.

It's not the first time eminent domain fears have been raised around AI data centers

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While Ohioans have rejected the building of new data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future. That's if a newly leaked bill that could allow data centers to be classified as public utilities is allowed to progress. The move would see the list of who can qualify for eminent domain law expanded, moving beyond entities owned or operated by municipal corporations, electric cooperatives, and agencies holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The bill, leaked to WCPO Cincinnati, would add "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities."

Legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power company, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one. The writing has been on the wall for a while, too, after it was discovered in June that the Ohio Business Roundtable trade group recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law to "extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.”

This follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for new transmission lines needed to power new data centers. The law gives the government the power to take private land without the need for the owner's consent, so long as it is for public use and the owner receives appropriate compensation. The government can also delegate the same land-grabbing power to “private entities or common carriers,” which includes utility companies.

This is already happening, too. Earlier this year, the largest utility company in Georgia required the removal of 30 residential properties in order to upgrade its grid. Residents claimed that the expansion was to power AI data centers, a fact given more weight by the fact that one such data center was located just a few miles away.

Despite this, eminent domain law can still be used for good. Nashville set out to use the same law to block the building of a 69,220-square-foot single-story data center next to a zoo. Nashville Metro Council approved the use of eminent domain as a way to buy the land from a local developer who planned the $700 million data center buildout.

#10683. When Should You Remove NAT from an On-Prem Kubernetes Network?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

In an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads. But direct routing is not automatically the right choice.

The decision depends on what the organization controls and what it needs from the network. A team that owns the physical fabric, has enough address space, and is comfortable operating BGP may benefit from making pod networks directly routable. A smaller environment, a team without control of the underlay, or a cluster that benefits from network abstraction may be better served by NAT or an overlay.

Kubernetes is also changing the ground under these decisions: kube-proxy is set to drop IPVS support starting with version 1.43, with nftables as the replacement. For on-prem teams already reviewing their service data path, it is a good moment to ask whether NAT still belongs in it.

So the useful question is not how to eliminate NAT, but when the operational benefits of doing so justify the additional routing responsibility.

NAT solves a real problem. It allows an internal network to use its own address space without requiring the surrounding infrastructure to know how to reach every endpoint inside it. This is especially useful when you don’t control the underlying network.

However, an on-premises data center is different. When you control both the Kubernetes cluster and the surrounding physical network, you can make Kubernetes networks directly routable.

In our case, removing NAT had practical and architectural benefits. It improved network performance, reduced CPU load on the nodes, and removed the risk of conntrack tables filling up on Kubernetes hosts. A directly routed L3 model also works well for traffic balancing when a node has two uplinks.

This does not mean eliminating NAT from the data center entirely. NAT can remain at the boundary of the on-premises network, for example on hardware firewalls. Inside the data center, however, Kubernetes networks can be directly routable, allowing the physical network to reach workloads using the same routing mechanisms it already uses elsewhere.

In our implementation, BGP connects the Kubernetes network to the data center fabric: BIRD runs on the nodes and advertises pod CIDRs and selected service addresses, while kube-router manages Kubernetes networking. We described this implementation in more detail in our earlier article on building a routable on-prem

Kubernetes cluster with BGP and ECMP. The important point for this decision is not the particular stack, but the requirement it creates: the surrounding network must be able to accept and route Kubernetes prefixes safely. If the organization cannot or does not want to make the cluster part of its routing domain, keeping NAT or an overlay is usually the simpler choice.

Removing NAT alone does not make a network resilient. If every node still depends on one switch, one NIC, or one uplink, direct routing simply exposes the same physical single point of failure more clearly.

The resilience benefit appears when the physical topology supports multiple independent paths. In our setup, nodes connect to independent data center switches and ECMP can use equivalent routes across those paths. If one path disappears, traffic can continue over the other.

That distinction matters when deciding whether direct routing is worth the effort. Organizations with redundant uplinks and switches can integrate Kubernetes into an already resilient routed fabric. If the underlay itself has no path redundancy, removing NAT should not be presented as a high-availability improvement: the physical failure domain still dominates the design.

Our stack is one example of how direct routing can be implemented, not a default recommendation for clusters that remove NAT. We chose kube-router because it supports a minimal installation as a binary and systemd service and covers the networking functions we need for this L3 design. BIRD handles route advertisements to the surrounding network.

Other environments may reasonably choose Calico for conventional L3 routing or Cilium when an eBPF-based dataplane and its additional capabilities are useful. The choice of CNI and routing daemon is secondary to the architectural decision: first decide whether exposing Kubernetes prefixes to the physical network makes operational sense, then choose the implementation that fits the team’s requirements.

A directly routed Kubernetes network is not automatically better than an overlay or NAT-based architecture. Each model solves a different operational problem.

NAT is a reasonable choice when the cluster needs to remain isolated from the surrounding address plan, when pod addresses cannot be routed through the data center, or when the infrastructure team does not control the upstream network. It also keeps Kubernetes-specific prefixes out of the physical routing domain, which can be valuable for smaller environments where direct visibility into every pod is not important.

An overlay is useful when portability and abstraction matter more than exposing the physical packet path. It lets Kubernetes networking remain largely independent of the underlay and can simplify deployment across heterogeneous infrastructure. The tradeoff is another layer to inspect during troubleshooting and, depending on the implementation, encapsulation overhead.

Direct routing makes the most sense when the organization owns the physical network, has address space available for pod CIDRs, and has operators comfortable with BGP and route filtering. It becomes more attractive when preserving source addresses, using standard network troubleshooting tools, predictable performance, or integrating the cluster with redundant data center paths are important. At a larger scale, those operational benefits can justify the extra coordination between Kubernetes and network teams.

The broader lesson is not that every Kubernetes cluster needs BGP or that NAT should disappear everywhere. It is that Kubernetes has matured enough that we should stop automatically treating its network as a black box.

As more production and AI workloads move onto Kubernetes, network architecture becomes part of application reliability. In an on-premises data center, BGP and ECMP give us the option to use the resilience already available in the physical network rather than building another isolated networking layer on top of it.

Sometimes the best way to make Kubernetes networking more robust is not to add another abstraction, but to remove one. But only when the surrounding infrastructure and the team operating it are ready to take responsibility for the routing that abstraction previously hid.

If most of those answers are yes, direct routing is worth serious consideration. If not, NAT or an overlay may be the more resilient operational choice—not because it is technically more advanced, but because it better matches the environment.

#10681. What it takes to pivot

There comes a time when many companies need to pivot. Maybe you want to expand out of your core category into a new one, or maybe you’re making a complete 180. When I joined You.com as COO in January this year, we decided to pivot by consolidating our product and business units around one core offering. Frankly, that offering had always been the heart of the company. This decision came down to evaluating three dimensions of the business: people, products, and customers.

From first-hand experience, I can tell you that how you approach a pivot’s first 90 days can make or break your business. When done ineffectively, it can leave employees and customers uncertain. When done well, you can bring both of those groups on board, united under a new vision.

Here are three tips for how to have a successful company pivot, from someone who recently navigated it.

1. ARRIVE WITH A THESIS, THEN TRY TO BREAK IT

Whether you’re coming into a company for the first time like I did, or you’re a long-time team member, you should always be evaluating its strengths and weaknesses to inform the best next steps to take. I wasn’t trying to shake things up for the sake of change. Rather, I had a series of conversations with the founder and CEO before I even stepped foot in the door that shaped my initial vision and plan for the company’s future. I developed an initial thesis for how the company should move forward. But rather than immediately implementing my ideas, I used the first 30 days to test it, finding its gaps and strengths. When exploring a pivot, keep an open mind and gauge buy-in before making any major changes.

I spent my first 30 days diving into the people, product, and customers. I took dozens of one-on-one meetings with employees from all departments and levels, spent enough hands-on time with the products to understand them, and also spoke with dozens of customers about what they liked about the products or how they would change them.

I looked at the company the way an investor would from the outside. I asked questions like: Where are we best positioned to win short-term and long-term? Where do we have true competitive advantage? Where is the best market opportunity? Where are our best win rates? Where is our biggest pipeline? Where is our best retention? Even if these answers differ from your original ideas, ego can’t change the data. These efforts validated my initial thesis and gave me the data and examples to commit to the pivot.

2. PIVOT AROUND A NORTH STAR

Teams are much more receptive in a return to the mission or reinforcement of the mission rather than a reinvention. You want to frame your pivot around a central anchor point, informed by the data. Another way to think of it is to clarify your North Star and pinpoint the business’s strengths and barriers to success.  

At You.com, we had success because like most companies, we made things that customers were willing to pay for. We also went out of our way to find solutions to specific problems they were facing. This is all positive, and in the process we made good products.

The reality was we sometimes built custom solutions for different customers which were valuable but not scalable. That’s not to say we shouldn’t have pursued it. Companies should branch out, test new ideas, and find creative solutions to new problems. Throughout this process, though, the outcome needs to serve the business’s North Star and value-creation objectives.

In our case, a pivot wasn’t completely revamping the product or service. Rather, we realized that the web search API product line was our foundation, and contributed to the majority of our revenues. However, it was not getting the majority of resources. We made the informed decision to reorient our company around this core product and went all-in.

This pivot essentially brought us home. When the company launched in 2021, we were the first to introduce LLMs in a search engine context. A year later, we were the first to connect an LLM to the web and started building the foundation for how AI uses the internet. From this, we developed easier ways for businesses to plug their AI into the web. Over time, we added different layers and custom-built different capabilities. But the pivot was to remove the layers and focus on the foundation.

If you’re facing a similar decision, go back to the people, product, and customer. If what’s working is 90% of the business, make it 100% of the business. If the energy comes from removal, and you give it an earnest shot to build the one thing you know you’re good at, watch what happens to the entire organization.

3. CREATE A SOFT LANDING FOR WHAT GETS LEFT

It’s important not to trivialize the 10% that gets removed, because those customers bought from us for a specific reason. Telling those customers we were moving on was delicate. Those relationships took years to build and I wanted them to feel honored on the way out.

Just like you found creative solutions to their original problems, continue to do that now. In our case, we spun out a joint venture with a professional services partner who could continue supporting businesses with custom-built solutions. Those customers had somewhere to go and didn’t get abandoned. And we could focus all the company resources around a core product.

Ninety days of listening and designing bought the next 90 days of full-speed work. People become aligned because you listened. The product is there because it’s what you are excited about and what you do best. The customer trusts you because you showed them focus, authenticity, and caring.

Alex Triplett is COO of You.com.

#10677. ANT update: Anthropic stock opens higher in Nasdaq debut

Update Thursday, 12:35 p.m.

Shares of Anthropic, PBC opened at $111.50 on Thursday in the year’s most hyped stock market debut. That’s roughly 34% higher than the $83 share price set before trading began—itself an increase over the AI giant’s original target range.

However, the stock quickly began to fall in the first hour and was trading at around $99 a share as of this writing.

Much of the market also moved lower, with the Nasdaq down around 0.73% as of 12:40 p.m. ET.

Original story:

Today, the most hyped IPO of the year (and that’s saying something) is expected to finally take place.

Claude LLM maker Anthropic, PBC (Nasdaq: ANT) will debut on the Nasdaq to much fanfare and lofty expectations. But while the Nasdaq opens at 9:30 a.m. ET, it’s likely Anthropic’s shares will not begin trading to the general public until later.

Here’s what you need to know.

The largest IPO in history

Today is Anthropic’s market debut, and its shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The initial public offering is the largest in history, surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June. The AI giant raised $81.3 billion in the offering.

The forthcoming stock listing is also the most-hyped of the year.

As Fast Company previously noted, Anthropic is considered a pure-play AI company. That is, the company’s sole business is artificial intelligence, as opposed to, say, SpaceX, which is mainly a space transportation and telecommunications company first, and an AI company second.

As the largest pure-play AI IPO ever, there’s a lot riding on how the shares react. If investors scoop them up and the share price pops, it could suggest that Wall Street still has an appetite for riskier AI-related stocks, despite recent pullbacks in the broader tech market.

However, don’t expect to know how ANT shares are performing as soon as the Nasdaq opens at 9:30 a.m. ET. That’s because, despite the market open, the first buy and sell orders for ANT shares likely won’t be fulfilled until later in the day.

What time do Anthropic’s shares begin trading today?

If a stock is already listed on an exchange, its shares usually begin trading to the public as soon as that exchange opens. But for market debuts, things are a little different.

Stock exchanges know that there is frequently a flurry of orders (both buy and sell) when a hot stock debuts.

If the stock were to trade immediately when the market opened, it could cause extreme price volatility, sending the stock up or down significantly in a matter of seconds. Another reason is operational: Nasdaq simply needs time to match orders—buyers with sellers—and determine a price.

Because of this, markets like the Nasdaq have procedures in place that delay trading by a little bit so buyers and sellers can get a better idea of demand and price the stock accordingly. Nasdaq calls this a Halt Cross.

Only once Nasdaq has determined an opening clearing price based on all its buy and sell orders does it release the stock for trading.

Why does this sound familiar?

If this sounds familiar, it’s because it’s exactly the same process that happened with the SpaceX IPO.

While SPCX shares debuted on the Nasdaq on June 12, they did not begin trading immediately when the Nasdaq opened at 9:30 a.m. ET. Instead, SpaceX’s shares began trading about two to three hours after the morning bell.

So, what time, then, will Anthropic’s shares actually begin trading on the Nasdaq?

It’s impossible to say for sure. Nasdaq’s rules don’t restrict the Halt Cross to a certain defined period, such as two hours. The Halt Cross lasts as long as it needs to.

However, if history is any indication, the Halt Cross usually ends anywhere from 2-4 hours after markets open.

That rough estimate suggests that Anthropic shares will begin trading at some point roughly between 11:30 a.m. ET and 1:30 p.m. ET today.

#10676. YouTube ‘Co-Views’ try to guess how many people are watching your TV, rolling out now

Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

Now, YouTube says it might count more views with a new “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

In a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change.

YouTube says it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”

How is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”

The most highly anticipated video game of the decade is here. GTA VI arrives almost 13 years after GTA V, with reports suggesting that it has already generated around $1.54 billion in revenue from 16 million preorders. Ahead of its release, Rockstar Games has finally shared some technical details, including rendering resolutions and upscaling technologies being used across all consoles.

In a statement shared with Wccftech, the technical team at Rockstar has confirmed that GTA VI uses different upscaling solutions across all consoles in order to achieve a balance between visual quality and performance with a target of 30FPS. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use Rockstar's own temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) solution, while the PlayStation 5 Pro relies on Sony's second-generation PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR2). The Xbox Series S, meanwhile, relies on AMD's FSR 4 upscaling technology.

As for rendered resolutions, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and PlayStation 5 Pro all start with a native base resolution of 1440p, which is then upscaled to 4K. The Xbox Series S is the least powerful console; thus, the game runs at a lower base resolution of 720p, which is upscaled to 1080p using FSR 4. The final image on all consoles is then composited with a 4K user interface before being presented.

Rockstar has also developed a physically-based material library for GTA VI and a cinematic imaging pipeline to deliver realistic lighting, reflections, and material details within the game. The team says it has worked to maintain a consistent lighting solution across all consoles, including the Xbox Series S, while adjusting ray-traced global illumination (RTGI) features depending on each platform's hardware capabilities.

The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S launched all the way back in 2020, and while the consoles have capable hardware, their architectures are finally beginning to show their age. The fact that Rockstar is targeting just 30FPS across all consoles, while relying on different upscaling technologies and rendering resolutions, highlights how much performance is potentially being left on the table in order to maintain visual fidelity. That being said, a PC release of GTA VI continues to be a big question mark. Rockstar is yet to announce a release date or even provide a launch window, meaning that PC gamers can only rely on Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream the game on their systems.

#10673. The real lesson businesses should learn from video games (it’s more than ‘gamification’)

In the early 2000s I (Bing) found myself crouched in an office cubicle frantically scribbling down a few things I thought the video game industry could teach a burgeoning online bookstore.

I was initially reluctant when my friend, the legendary venture capitalist John Doerr, asked me to take a meeting in Seattle with a buzzy, young startup CEO. I was a midcareer video game executive and this particular founder had already been named Time’s 1999 person of the year. Terrified to look a fool, I ducked into a cubicle at the Electronic Arts office in Seattle and outlined an idea for an online customer loyalty program based on the strategy that had turned Madden NFL into a forever franchise by giving gamers reasons to come back year after year.

I practically stuffed the one-pager in Jeff Bezos’s hand the first time we met over coffee. He laughed, but indulged me and unfurled the page. I started my career in video games as a marketing chief, and I was still in the habit of writing headline copy for all my one-pagers. Across the top of this one I wrote: Amazon Prime.

Jeff would say that Prime’s success was a good surprise, but when you know video games, when you understand the magical ways that they tap into our intrinsic motivations and make us want to come back again and again, you understand that game design thinking has the potential to increase retention and engagement in almost any walk of life. After Amazon Prime worked so well, I brought the lessons of video games to all kinds of consumer industries, from entertainment products like Spotify to financial products like Better Mortgage to educational products like Coursera and Duolingo and even weight loss apps like My Fitness Pal.

A bad rap

I used to call the craft of applying video game design to consumer products “video gamification,” but these days gamification has a bad rap. Some of the smartest business minds I know brush it off as a short-lived 2010s trend that didn’t pan out. I’ve heard countless product teams complain that the points and leaderboard systems they build into their user interfaces didn’t make a dent in any of their retention metrics. Worse still, I have friends and peers who recoil when they hear the word “gamify,” immediately assuming someone is trying to manipulate their time and attention. Gamification has taken on such a negative connotation that I’ve stopped using the word altogether.

The thing is, the so-called “gamification” trend that failed hard in the 2010s was based on a fundamental misunderstanding of what makes successful games work. Product teams that couldn’t figure out how to boost traffic to their app would probably be surprised to learn that successful games rarely rely on competition to motivate players. In fact, in video games, cooperation is a far more important mechanism than competition.

Connection, mastery, productivity

If you’re going to channel the motivational magic of a great game, you need to understand what actually goes into crafting one. The top reasons that players come back to a game are, in order of importance, social connection, personal mastery, and productivity. Most business execs I meet assume that productivity measures like money and rankings are the most important motivational forces, but the video game industry has found for decades that social relationships and the satisfaction of self-improvement far outweigh them.

In the early days of the Facebook juggernaut game Farmville, its developer, Zynga, found that the notifications that invited friends to play cooperatively garnered 30 times the clicks that the competitive, brag-based notifications did. In games, a two-way social interaction is the top predictor of whether or not somebody comes back tomorrow.

Nongamers find this surprising, but they shouldn’t! We’re human beings, ever motivated to build communities and deepen our relationships with one another. We come back to the games and products that best align with that. One of the great social features of the business networking platform Linkedin is “Endorsements,” where users are invited to publicly vouch for their peers and strengthen their professional relationships. Cooperative features like this give people a reason to return to the résumé sharing platform regularly, even when they aren’t searching for jobs.

Personal mastery and self-improvement are also intrinsic motivators to every gamer. Mechanics that give people a framework to measure and track self-improvement, like experience points and level-ups, create an invigorating sense of progress with each session. Scores are important in games, but more so as a way to rate individual progression instead of rank it against others.

Productivity measures like time saved and money earned also motivate us, especially when they’re paired with our social and mastery priorities. We like earning money, sure, but we love earning money doing things we already wanted to do, and we might forgo it when it comes in direct conflict with our social relationships and sense of self-worth.

More of what they want

Amazon Prime works because it gives its customers more of what they already want. Free and fast shipping offers an incredible productivity proposition, especially in terms of time saved, and individualized customer profiles help us form identities around ourselves as consumers. Amazon knows that one of the biggest predictors of whether a Prime user renews is how often they use their subscription benefits, but pushing members to make purchases they otherwise wouldn’t risks undermining long-term loyalty. So Amazon treats Prime like a forever game franchise, continually improving the experience and layering on new benefits like Prime Video, Amazon Music, and prescription savings. Each gives members another reason to use their subscription in ways that already align with their interests.

When I gut check a user experience to see if it’s aligned with my own wants and needs, it’s usually as simple as asking, does this product like me? Do I feel better about myself at the end of my session than I did at the beginning? If the answer is no, it usually means the designers are trying to gamify me against my own best interest, like a credit card rewards program that persuades me to spend more money than I would otherwise, or a social media platform that delivers empty dopamine hits without any meaningful upside to my social relationships.

These days, I’ve dropped the term “gamification,” but my belief in applying game thinking to products hasn’t wavered. Start with what people actually want, and build around those priorities. You’ll tap into intrinsic motivations far more powerful than any user interface trick or attention hack. That’s real video gamification, and that will always work.
